original_interpretation: JCT estimated that the semiconductor investment credit proposed in the Build Back Better Act would cost US$10.2 billion over FY2022-FY2031, of which US$5.6 billion would be outlays from direct pay.
evidence_found: "The Joint Committee on Taxation (JCT) estimated this credit would reduce federal tax revenues by $10.2 billion over the FY2022-FY2031 budget window, with $5.6 billion of that total associated with outlays due to direct pay." (CRS Insight IN11923, May 11, 2022, section "Semiconductor Tax Credits Proposed in the 117th Congress"); the credit is the one in "The House-passed and Senate Finance Committee's version of the Build Back Better Act (H.R. 5376)".
notes: Figures, fiscal-year window and the Build Back Better (not enacted 48D) scope match. Historical estimate for a proposal that was never enacted in that form; claim_type estimate is correct.

original_interpretation: As of July 2025 Commerce had made CHIPS incentive awards to 19 companies for 40 projects, totalling US$30.9 billion in direct funding plus US$5.5 billion in loans to two of them (US$36.4 billion), excluding the Secure Enclave.
evidence_found: "As of July 2025, the Department of Commerce has provided incentive awards to 19 companies for 40 projects ... In total, Commerce awarded the 19 companies with $30.9 billion in direct funding and two of them with $5.5 billion in loans through the incentive awards." (GAO-26-107882, Highlights); Table 2 (p. 12) "Total 40 $30,938 $5,500 $36,438". Newer: "With these new awards, Commerce has awarded a total of 24 companies approximately $31.7 billion in direct funding for 49 projects ... as well as workforce activities" and "Commerce has now awarded a total of three companies $6.8 billion in loans." (GAO-26-109121, section "Commerce Awarded Nine Additional Projects Since July 2025", footnote 15; as of July 15, 2026)
correction: Accurate as of July 2025, but superseded: as of 15 July 2026 GAO reports 24 companies, 49 projects, about US$31.7 billion direct funding and US$6.8 billion in loans to three companies (new awards to USA Rare Earth, Bosch, Crucible Metals, Vulcan Elements, Powerex).
notes: The US$30.9bn includes US$296m for workforce activities (p. 11). Added superseding claim.

original_interpretation: The US$30.9 billion of CHIPS direct funding awarded by July 2025 represented 89 percent of the US$34.7 billion available for direct funding (excluding US$3.5 billion Secure Enclave and US$770 million of administrative, sequestration and transfer allocations).
evidence_found: "The direct funding awards represent 89 percent of the $34.7 billion in available funds for direct funding." Footnote 25: "The $34.7 billion does not include funding available for the Secure Enclave program ($3.5 billion), which is outside the scope of this report, nor $770 million of required allocations for administrative expenses, sequestration reductions, and statutory transfers." (GAO-26-107882, p. 11). Newer: "This represents approximately 89 percent of the $35.5 billion available for the incentives program." (GAO-26-109121, as of July 15, 2026; footnote 16 excludes only the $3.5 billion Secure Enclave)
correction: Accurate as of July 2025. GAO's August 2026 report puts cumulative direct funding (about US$31.7bn, 24 companies) at about 89 percent of US$35.5 billion available (a different denominator that excludes only the Secure Enclave).
notes: Both reports give 89 percent but on different bases (US$34.7bn vs US$35.5bn); not a contradiction, a changed denominator. Added superseding claim.

original_interpretation: The CHIPS Act set aside US$6 billion of the US$39 billion to support up to US$75 billion in loans and loan guarantees.
evidence_found: "The CHIPS Act appropriated $6 billion of the $39 billion to support up to $75 billion in loans and loan guarantees." (GAO-26-107882, footnote 17, p. 9)

original_interpretation: GAO's July 2025 awardee table shows Micron with US$6.440 billion of direct funding for 5 projects, TSMC US$6.565 billion plus US$5.0 billion loans for 3 projects (31.7% of all funding), and Intel US$7.865 billion for 6 projects (21.6%).
evidence_found: Table 2 (p. 12): "Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company 3 $6,565 $5,000 $11,565 31.7%"; "Intel 6 $7,865 — $7,865 21.6%"; "Micron 5 $6,440 — $6,440 17.7%" (GAO-26-107882, "Semiconductor Incentive Awardees, as of July 2025")
notes: Matches exactly (USD m, includes workforce funding). The table is a July 2025 snapshot: Intel's award was amended in August 2025 (equity stake of 9.9 percent; milestones removed, projects complete once Intel spends the award amount), per GAO-26-109121, so Intel's current terms differ.

original_interpretation: CHIPS incentive awards cover between 4.6 and 38.8 percent of projects' company-estimated capital expenditures, with a median of 14.2 percent (as of July 2025).
evidence_found: "Awards only cover a portion of the projects' total expected capital expenditures, ranging from 4.6 to 38.8 percent, with a median of 14.2 percent (see fig. 4)." (GAO-26-107882, pp. 12-13); Fig. 4 note: "Projected capital expenditures are estimated by companies ... capital expenditure data for three projects from the same company were only available combined. We treated those three projects as one project"
notes: Figure relates to facility funding (Fig. 4 title) and excludes post-July 2025 amendments. Population of 38 units is correct.

original_interpretation: The first CHIPS funding notice said direct funding would generally cover 5 to 15 percent of a project's capital expenditures and total support including loans up to 35 percent; the statute caps awards at US$3 billion per project absent extra certification and reporting.
evidence_found: "The first notice of funding opportunity stated that direct funding awards would generally cover 5 to 15 percent of capital expenditures, and all awards (including the principal amount of loans and loan guarantees) would generally cover up to 35 percent." ... "by not providing more than $3 billion for any individual project, as called for by the FY21 NDAA." Footnote 41: "The FY21 NDAA requires additional consultation, certification, and reporting to exceed such award amount." (GAO-26-107882, p. 24)
notes: Statute requires consultation as well as certification and reporting to exceed US$3bn; GAO notes one project initially exceeded US$3bn and was later amended below it.

original_interpretation: As of July 2025 Commerce had disbursed US$6 billion of CHIPS incentive funding, having verified 18 of 35 disbursement requests.
evidence_found: "As of July 2025, Commerce has reviewed and verified completion of 18 of 35 disbursement requests, and it has disbursed $6 billion." (GAO-26-107882, p. 18). Newer: "As of April 2026, Commerce disbursed $13.1 billion to awardees. This was approximately 42 percent of the total $31.2 billion in direct funding awards Commerce had made as of April 2026." (GAO-26-109121, section "Commerce Disbursed $13 Billion as of April 2026")
correction: Superseded: US$13.1 billion disbursed as of April 2026 (about 42 percent of US$31.2 billion direct funding awarded by then), including Intel disbursements under its amended agreement.
notes: The 35 requests include 11 for workforce activities. GAO-26-109121's Highlights say '$31.5 billion' while the body says '$31.2 billion' as of April 2026; internal inconsistency in GAO's text. Added superseding claim.

original_interpretation: CHIPS award documents set 161 milestones across the 40 projects; as of July 2025 companies had reported completion of 24.
evidence_found: "Commerce award documents identify 161 total milestones across the 40 projects." ... "Commerce officials stated that companies have submitted reports of milestone completion for 24 of 161 milestones, as of July 2025." (GAO-26-107882, p. 17)
notes: Strictly, companies had submitted completion reports for 24 (per Commerce officials). GAO-26-109121 reports that as of April 2026, excluding Intel, 'Eleven awardees received disbursements for completing 24 project milestones' with 125 still in progress, so the snapshot remains consistent.

original_interpretation: One CHIPS project, a leading-edge logic fab in Phoenix, Arizona that began construction before the CHIPS Act, was certified complete in June 2025; its award was US$2.9 billion.
evidence_found: "One project, a new leading-edge logic chip manufacturing facility in Phoenix, Arizona, which started construction prior to the enactment of the CHIPS Act according to information on the company's website, was certified as complete in June 2025. The company received a $2.9 billion award for the project." (GAO-26-107882, p. 17)
notes: GAO does not name the company (implicitly TSMC Arizona Fab 21 phase 1); pre-CHIPS construction start is per the company's website as cited by GAO.

original_interpretation: CHIPS disbursements are effectively reimbursements after proof of milestone completion, and Commerce may claw back part or all of disbursed funds if milestones and other terms are not met.
evidence_found: "Commerce disburses funding to awardees after proof of milestone completion, according to officials. Disbursements are in effect reimbursements to companies, which front the project costs until milestones are completed. If companies do not complete certain milestones and other terms, Commerce may require partial or full repayment of funds previously disbursed, referred to as clawbacks." (GAO-26-107882, p. 18)
notes: Describes the standard structure; Intel's August 2025 amendment departs from it (disbursement on cost incurred, milestones removed) per GAO-26-109121.

original_interpretation: Commerce negotiated upside-sharing agreements for 27 of the 40 CHIPS projects; profit thresholds ranged from about US$3 million to US$29.2 billion (median US$7.7 billion) and the government's share of excess profit from about 2 to 31 percent (median 22 percent).
evidence_found: "Commerce obtained upside sharing agreements for 27 of the 40 awarded projects." ... "The first profit threshold at which a project's upside sharing agreements would go into effect ranged from approximately $3 million to $29.2 billion, with a median of $7.7 billion.38 Percentage of profit to be shared with the federal government ranged from approximately 2 percent to 31 percent, with a median of 22 percent.39" Footnote 38: "This analysis is based on 21 of the 27 projects"; footnote 39: "based on 25 of the 27 projects" (GAO-26-107882, p. 23)
notes: Threshold stats cover 21 of 27 projects and percentage stats 25 of 27 (others to be determined). As of July 2025; GAO-26-109121 reports upside-sharing was later removed for two projects and revised for a third.

original_interpretation: The CHIPS funding notice required upside-sharing agreements for projects receiving more than US$150 million of direct funding, with limited exceptions, and Commerce stated upside sharing is generally not expected to be triggered because thresholds are well above projected profits.
evidence_found: "The notice of funding opportunity states that upside sharing agreements would be required for all projects receiving greater than $150 million in direct funding, with limited exceptions." ... "However, Commerce has stated that upside sharing is generally not expected to occur, because thresholds are significantly above projected profits." (GAO-26-107882, pp. 23-24)

original_interpretation: Commerce estimates its funded projects will raise the US share of global leading-edge logic chip manufacturing from 0 percent in 2022 to 20 percent by 2030.
evidence_found: "Commerce estimates that these projects will bring the U.S. share of global leading-edge logic chip manufacturing from 0 percent in 2022 to 20 percent by 2030." (GAO-26-107882, Highlights)
notes: Correctly typed as an estimate (a Commerce projection relayed by GAO, not a GAO finding).

original_interpretation: The 40 CHIPS projects are in 19 states; Arizona, New York and Texas host 20 of the projects and US$26.7 billion of the US$36.4 billion facility funding.
evidence_found: "The projects are located in 19 states. Arizona, New York, and Texas account for half of the projects (20 of 40) and nearly three-quarters of facility funding ($26.7 billion of $36.4 billion)." (GAO-26-107882, p. 13)
notes: As of July 2025; GAO-26-109121 Fig. 1 updates project funding by location as of July 15, 2026 (49 projects).

original_interpretation: From January 2025 through April 2026 Commerce negotiated amendments to CHIPS incentive award agreements with 14 awardees, which among other things removed childcare requirements and gave more flexibility in allocating funds across activities.
evidence_found: "From January 2025 through April 2026, Commerce negotiated amendments to award agreements with 14 awardees." ... "Additionally, nine awardees reached agreement with Commerce on amendments related to their funded workforce activities. These amendments added detail to the description of when awardees should submit progress reports, removed requirements related to providing childcare for employees, and provided additional flexibility in how awardees may allocate funds across different activities." (GAO-26-109121, section "Commerce Amended Awards for Most Recipients")
notes: The childcare and fund-allocation changes were in the workforce-activity amendments of nine of the 14 awardees, not necessarily all 14.

original_interpretation: Two CHIPS incentive award amendments involved equity: Intel's gave Commerce 9.9 percent of its shares (valued at US$8.9 billion) and an unnamed second company's gave Commerce a warrant to purchase equity; upside-sharing was removed for two projects and revised for a third.
evidence_found: "Two amendments involved equity agreements. Intel's agreement was amended to provide Commerce with 9.9 percent of outstanding shares, which was valued at $8.9 billion at the time. [20] A second company's agreement was amended to provide Commerce with a warrant to purchase equity. [21] In addition, upside-sharing agreements were removed for two projects and revised for a third project." (GAO-26-109121, "Equity and Profit-Sharing Changes")

original_interpretation: Commerce cancelled CHIPS R&D awards representing US$7.8 billion of the US$11 billion appropriated for advanced microelectronics R&D, including the Natcast NSTC award (August 2025) and SRC's Manufacturing USA institute award (terminated for convenience, December 2025), and paused or cancelled NAPMP awards.
evidence_found: "Commerce initially established key aspects of the programs but later canceled awards representing approximately $7.8 billion of the $11 billion appropriated (see fig. 4)."; "In August 2025, Commerce took its first step in changing its approach to the NSTC by sending a letter to Natcast canceling its award."; "In December 2025, Commerce sent a letter to SRC terminating the award for convenience."; "Commerce also canceled or paused NAPMP awards" (GAO-26-109121)
notes: GAO says 'approximately' US$7.8bn. Natcast's award was US$7.4bn.

original_interpretation: Factoring in cancellations, Commerce had expended US$506.8 million, about 5 percent of the US$11 billion CHIPS R&D appropriation, as of GAO's August 2026 report.
evidence_found: "Factoring in the cancellations, Commerce has expended $506.8 million, approximately 5 percent of the $11 billion in appropriated funds for the advanced microelectronics R&D programs." (GAO-26-109121)
notes: Breakdown: about US$347.3m internal agency research, US$79.2m admin, US$64.1m on a canceled award, US$16.1m other.

original_interpretation: Since September 2025 Commerce made three new CHIPS R&D awards totalling US$900 million, each with equity for Commerce: xLight US$150 million (alternative EUV light source), SandboxAQ US$500 million (AI for materials) and I-Pulse US$250 million (silicon-carbide devices).
evidence_found: "Since September 2025, Commerce has made three new awards totaling $900 million and nine preliminary awards ... First, Commerce awarded $150 million in direct funding to xLight to support development of an alternative light source for extreme ultraviolet (EUV) lithography. ... Second, Commerce awarded $500 million in direct funding to SandboxAQ to use artificial intelligence in the development of new and alternative materials for semiconductor manufacturing. Third, Commerce awarded $250 million in direct funding to I-Pulse to develop novel silicon-carbide semiconductors to operate in harsh environments. As part of the award agreements, the three companies will provide Commerce with equity." (GAO-26-109121)
notes: I-Pulse purpose is SiC devices for harsh environments.

original_interpretation: GAO reports that nine preliminary quantum-computing awards made with CHIPS R&D funds will also include equity agreements.
evidence_found: "The nine preliminary awards total approximately $2 billion for quantum computing, and Commerce has stated that they will also include equity agreements." (GAO-26-109121)
notes: The equity statement is Commerce's, relayed by GAO; the awards are preliminary and 'using or intending to use' Section 9906 R&D funds. Total about US$2bn.

original_interpretation: GAO recommended that Commerce's CHIPS R&D Office develop a plan and timeline showing how and when each R&D programme will meet statutory requirements.
evidence_found: Recommendations: (1) "develops a plan and timeline with sufficient detail to address how and when the National Semiconductor Technology Center will align with all applicable requirements in the FY21 NDAA"; (2) "fully implements the NAPMP requirements by either (a) making a timely decision to move forward with the two existing awards or (b) developing a plan and timeline..."; (3) "develops a plan and timeline describing how and when Commerce will reestablish the Industrial Advisory Committee" (GAO-26-109121, Recommendations for Executive Action). Highlights: "Commerce agreed with the recommendations."
correction: GAO made three specific recommendations (NSTC plan and timeline; NAPMP decision on two existing awards or a plan; Industrial Advisory Committee plan), not a plan for each R&D programme. The Manufacturing USA institute and NIST research programme are not covered, and the advisory committee is not a programme.
notes: Added superseding claim.

original_interpretation: On 11 June 2025 Micron signed a CHIPS direct funding agreement of up to US$275 million for its Manassas, Virginia fab and amended its Idaho/New York agreements to add a second Boise fab, bringing its CHIPS grants to up to about US$6.4 billion.
evidence_found: "On June 11, 2025, we entered into amendments to the direct funding agreements to add a second planned fab in Boise, Idaho and allocated certain award funding from the $6.1 billion grants previously awarded to the second planned Idaho fab. The direct funding for up to $6.1 billion remains unchanged. On June 11, 2025, we also entered into a direct funding agreement with the U.S. Department of Commerce for up to $275 million in direct funding for our fab in Manassas, Virginia." ... "The grants under the funding agreements represent total CHIPS Act grants of up to $6.4 billion" (Micron FY2025 10-K, Government Incentives note, R27)

original_interpretation: Micron's CHIPS agreements allow ordinary recurring dividends but restrict special and one-time dividends for five years, cap share repurchases at Commerce-specified amounts in the first two years, and include clawbacks for missing agreed project completion dates.
evidence_found: "We are permitted to make customary and ordinary course recurring dividends (and reasonable ordinary course increases thereof) consistent with our past practice. There are restrictions on our payment of special and one-time dividends during the five-year period following the Idaho and New York award date of December 9, 2024. Share repurchases are permitted during the first two years of such five-year period up to amounts specified in the funding agreements to help offset the dilutive effects of employee stock compensation or as otherwise permitted by the U.S. Department of Commerce." ... "clawbacks related to the failure to complete a project by an agreed upon completion date" (Micron FY2025 10-K, R27)
notes: Five-year period runs from 9 Dec 2024; buybacks unrestricted in years 3-5 if conditions met. Clawbacks also cover foreign-country-of-concern violations and impermissible disposition.

original_interpretation: Micron discloses that under its CHIPS agreements it may owe upside-sharing amounts for up to ten years if cumulative project cash flows exceed specified thresholds, capped at 75% of award disbursements.
evidence_found: "We may be required to pay upside sharing amounts for a period of up to ten years following the first year in which the cumulative cash flow from a project is positive, if cumulative cash flows from the project exceed a threshold level that is at a significant premium to the baseline projection. The upside sharing amount would equal a modest sharing percentage of the excess cash flows above the threshold level, but not to exceed 75% of award disbursements for a project, after considering any clawbacks or other repayments." (Micron FY2025 10-K, R27)
notes: The 75% cap is per project, net of clawbacks/repayments.

original_interpretation: Government incentives related to capital expenditures had reduced Micron's property, plant and equipment by US$5.04 billion as of 28 August 2025, of which US$3.11 billion related to fiscal 2025 expenditures; these combine CHIPS grants, investment tax credits and non-US incentives.
evidence_found: "Government incentives related to capital expenditures have reduced property, plant and equipment by $5.04 billion as of August 28, 2025, of which $3.11 billion pertained to 2025 expenditures." "We receive incentives from governmental entities primarily in India, Japan, Singapore, and the United States principally in the form of cash grants and tax credits." (Micron FY2025 10-K, R27)
notes: Source does not split the US$5.04bn by CHIPS grant vs ITC vs non-US; the claim correctly says they are combined. Micron's FY2026 10-K (FY ending early Sep 2026) not found as of 2026-09-30.

original_interpretation: As of 28 August 2025 Micron reported US$5,206 million of not-yet-received US government incentive commitments subject to performance conditions, versus US$1,491 million in India, US$929 million in Japan and US$269 million in Singapore.
evidence_found: "we had the following commitments from various governmental entities, subject to achievement of certain performance conditions: As of August 28, 2025 U.S. $ 5,206 India 1,491 Japan 929 Singapore 269 Other 10 $ 7,905" (Micron FY2025 10-K, R27)
notes: Excludes receivables and cash already received, and excludes the 48D investment tax credit ('In addition to the U.S. commitment amount in the table above, we receive an investment tax credit'). A later Japan commitment of up to JPY500bn was finalized after year end.

original_interpretation: Wolfspeed announced on 1 December 2025 that it had received US$698.6 million of section 48D cash tax refunds from the IRS, part of about US$1 billion of 48D refunds it had accrued, after receiving US$186.5 million in fiscal 2025 for its fiscal 2023-2024 filings.
evidence_found: "Wolfspeed, Inc. (NYSE: WOLF) ... today announced that it has received $698.6 million in cash tax refunds from the Internal Revenue Service (IRS) from the Advanced Manufacturing Investment Credit (AMIC) under Section 48D of the Internal Revenue Code. The refund represents a significant step in the monetization of the approximately $1 billion of Section 48D cash tax refunds accrued from the AMIC. In fiscal 2025, the Company received $186.5 million in cash tax refunds related to its fiscal 2023 and fiscal 2024 federal tax filings." (Wolfspeed press release, December 1, 2025, paragraph 1; retrieved via WebFetch, curl blocked by Cloudflare)
notes: Company announcement; reported_claim and company_documentation classification are appropriate.

original_interpretation: Wolfspeed's 48D cash refunds (US$698.6 million received by December 2025, about US$1 billion accrued) exceed its never-finalised US$750 million CHIPS grant proposal, showing that for some firms the tax credit delivered more cash than the grant programme.
evidence_found: Component evidence: Wolfspeed: "received $698.6 million in cash tax refunds" and "approximately $1 billion of Section 48D cash tax refunds accrued"; "In fiscal 2025, the Company received $186.5 million" (SRC-0326). Wolfspeed US$750m proposal still preliminary as of 10 June 2026 per CLM-0933 (verified).
correction: US$698.6 million alone is below US$750 million. What exceeds the proposed grant is cumulative 48D cash received (US$186.5m in FY2025 plus US$698.6m in Dec 2025 = about US$885m) or the ~US$1bn accrued. The conclusion that the credit delivered more cash than the grant holds, since the grant paid nothing.
notes: Inference from CLM-1008 and CLM-0933. The release does not say whether the US$186.5m is inside the ~US$1bn accrued figure, so the two should not be added together. Added superseding inference.

original_interpretation: Wolfspeed's US$750 million CHIPS proposal was the largest not finalised before the change of administration in January 2025, and its shares fell by about half on 28 March 2025 amid doubts it would be paid.
evidence_found: "the very next day, Wolfspeed's stock plunged nearly in half, accounting for pretty much the entire month's losses ... That morning, rumors began circulating that the company would not receive the $750 million in CHIPS Act funding that the government had agreed to pay Wolfspeed during the prior administration." (Motley Fool, 7 Apr 2025, section "Layoffs, a new CEO, and CHIPS Act uncertainty")
correction: The article supports the ~50% drop on 28 March 2025 amid rumours about the US$750m. It does not say this was the largest proposal not finalised before January 2025; that part is unsupported by this source. It describes the funding as 'agreed to pay' and not yet disbursed.
notes: The researcher's paraphrase ('highest-dollar grant not officially awarded before Biden's exit') is not in the article text retrieved. Added superseding claim without the unsupported part.

original_interpretation: As of August 2026 Samsung was reported not yet to have received its US$4.745 billion CHIPS award, while Taylor Fab 1 trial production was expected to start around September 2026.
evidence_found: "Samsung's keep up the pace on works even as it's yet to receive the $4.745 billion CHIPS and Science Act funds that were granted to it by the previous administration in 2024." "Media reports from South Korea suggest that the trial production for Fab 1 may begin as early as next month, with the facility being operationalized before the end of 2026." (SamMobile, last updated August 19, 2026)
notes: Tier-3 news relaying Korean media, correctly typed reported_claim. The trial-production date is a media expectation ('may begin as early as'), not a Samsung statement. No newer source found by 2026-09-30 showing Samsung has received the funds.

original_interpretation: Under the CHIPS guardrails rule, a 'material expansion' of a facility in a foreign country of concern means increasing its capacity by more than five percent through added cleanroom, production line or other physical space; existing legacy-chip facilities may instead expand by ten percent over ten years.
evidence_found: "For existing facilities, material expansion means the increase of the semiconductor manufacturing capacity of an existing facility by more than five percent of the capacity memorialized in the required agreement due to the addition of a cleanroom, production line or other physical space, or a series of such additions. Any new construction of a facility for semiconductor manufacturing would also be a material expansion." ... "existing facilities that manufacture legacy semiconductors are permitted to increase capacity by ten percent over ten years from the award date." (NIST FAQ, "How will material expansion be measured?")
notes: Claim omits that building any new facility in a foreign country of concern is also a material expansion. Definition was revised by 88 Fed. Reg. 89,572 (15 C.F.R. 231).

original_interpretation: The CHIPS guardrails' technology clawback bars recipients from knowingly engaging in joint research or technology licensing with a foreign entity of concern on technology raising national security concerns, and a violation leads to recovery of the full award.
evidence_found: "the Technology Clawback, which prohibits a covered entity from knowingly engaging in any joint research or technology licensing effort with a foreign entity of concern that relates to a technology or product that raises national security concerns." ... "If there is a violation of the Technology Clawback by a covered entity, the full amount of the award will be recovered by the Department." (NIST FAQ)
notes: There is a safe harbour for ongoing activities memorialized in the award agreement.

original_interpretation: In July 2026 SEMI lobbied Congress for a multi-year extension of the 48D credit before its 31 December 2026 construction-start deadline and for eligibility to be widened to materials, specialty chemicals, gases and chip design, which are currently excluded.
evidence_found: "SEMI's primary request of Congress is a multi-year extension of Section 48D ahead of the December 31, 2026, construction deadline" ... "SEMI also urged Congress to consider strengthening the credit by expanding eligibility to cover the full semiconductor supply chain, including materials, specialty chemicals and gases, and design activities that are currently excluded." (I-Connect007, July 23, 2026, byline "SEMI", section "SEMI's Request")
notes: The article is a republished SEMI press release (byline SEMI); the original is on semi.org (industry_body). Expansion was a secondary 'consider' ask. As of 2026-09-30 the search found no enacted extension (H.R. 3204 BASIC Act, extending to 2030, still in committee).
